definition.text: Load balancing distributes a set of tasks, such as incoming network requests, across a set of computing resources so the work is processed more efficiently.

facts.text: Load balancing can improve response time and stops some nodes being overloaded while others sit idle.
Busy websites must serve hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of concurrent requests, and the cost-effective way to meet that volume is to add more servers.
A load balancer sits in front of the servers and routes each request to one able to handle it, so no single server is overworked enough to degrade performance.
If a server goes down, traffic is redirected to the remaining online servers; when a new server joins the group, requests start flowing to it automatically.
This supports horizontal scaling: extra servers are added to the pool and the load balancer spreads traffic across all of them.
Two main approaches exist: static algorithms ignore the state of the machines, while dynamic algorithms use it but need the machines to exchange information, risking lost efficiency.
Beyond parallel computing, load balancing is widely used to manage HTTP requests for sites with a large audience that must handle many requests per second.
Which algorithm fits depends on the nature of the tasks, the complexity, the hardware and the error tolerance required, so a compromise must be found for each application.

definition.text: A load balancer is a device or software application that distributes network or application traffic across multiple servers.

facts.text: For Internet services it is usually a software program listening on the port where external clients connect; it forwards each request to one of the backend servers.
The backend server usually replies through the balancer, so the client never learns about the internal separation of functions.
Because clients cannot contact backend servers directly, the internal network's structure stays hidden, which may protect against attacks on the servers' network stack or other services.
Its fundamental job is to distribute incoming requests over the backend servers of a cluster according to a scheduling algorithm.
Some balancers can forward to a backup balancer or show an outage message when all backend servers are unavailable.
ByteByteGo lists its roles as traffic distribution, high availability, SSL termination, session persistence, scalability and health monitoring.

title: Load balancing algorithms

definition.text: A load-balancing algorithm, also called a scheduling algorithm or load-balancing method, is the rule a load balancer uses to decide which backend server receives each request.

facts.text: Simple algorithms include random choice, round robin and least connections.

More sophisticated balancers weigh extra factors: a server's reported load, response times, up or down status from a monitoring poll, active connections, geographic location, capabilities, or how much traffic it recently received.
Singh's guide names round-robin, weighted round-robin, least connections, least response time, least bandwidth and hashing as the commonly used routing algorithms.
Least bandwidth measures traffic in megabits per second and sends each client request to the server currently carrying the least.
Power of two choices picks two servers at random and then chooses the better of the two.
ByteByteGo files round robin, sticky round-robin, weighted round-robin and hash as static algorithms, and least connections and least response time as dynamic ones.

conflicts.text: Lists least connections among the static load distribution methods.
conflicts.note: Wikipedia's 'Others' list sits under static distribution, but its own definition of static (c08acfe98f76) excludes system state, which least connections uses; ByteByteGo files it as dynamic.

notes: apparent inconsistency in Wikipedia: least connections (24eb2aca1aae) listed under static distribution though static is defined as ignoring system state (c08acfe98f76); ByteByteGo (8340a6800efe) files it as dynamic. The fact follows ByteByteGo; verification pass should check.

definition.text: Round robin sends requests to servers in turn, the first to the first server, the next to the second and so on to the last, then starts over.

facts.text: After the last server has had a request, assignment starts again from the first server.
The method can be weighted so that the most powerful units receive the largest number of requests, and receive them first.
It is one of the static methods, which work even when the execution time of tasks is not known in advance.
ByteByteGo notes that the services behind round robin are usually required to be stateless.

definition.text: Weighted round robin is round robin in which the administrator gives each server a weight, and servers with higher weights handle more requests.

facts.text: Singh describes it as building on round robin to account for differing server compute and traffic-handling capacity, using weights the administrator assigns, for example through DNS records.
Parallel infrastructures often mix units of different computing power, so lower-powered units may receive lighter requests, or fewer requests when request sizes are alike or unknown.
Many balancers let an operator assign a ratio so some backends get a greater share of the workload; this is a simple way to account for capacity differences, though it may not always work as desired.

title: Least connections

definition.text: Least connections sends each new request to the server that currently has the fewest active connections.

facts.text: The method can be weighted: each server's relative computing capacity is factored into deciding which one has the least connections.
Wikipedia counts it among the simple algorithms, alongside random choice and round robin.
ByteByteGo files it with the dynamic algorithms, next to least response time.

conflicts.text: Listed among the static load distribution methods.
conflicts.note: Wikipedia's 'Others' list sits under static distribution, but its own definition of static (c08acfe98f76) excludes system state; ByteByteGo files it as dynamic.

notes: apparent inconsistency in Wikipedia: 24eb2aca1aae places least connections under static distribution while c08acfe98f76 defines static as ignoring system state; the dynamic fact follows ByteByteGo (8340a6800efe). Verification pass should check.

definition.text: Least response time sends each new request to the service instance with the fastest response time.

facts.text: Singh describes it as picking the server by a formula that combines the fastest response time with the fewest active connections.
Wikipedia lists response times among the extra factors that sophisticated balancers consider, with reported load and up or down status.
ByteByteGo files it with the dynamic algorithms.

definition.text: Hash-based load balancing applies a hash function to a key such as the client IP address or request URL and routes the request to the server the result selects.

facts.text: The key is one the operator defines, such as the client IP address or the request URL.
Wikipedia lists it among the other assignment methods, describing it as allocating queries according to a hash table.
The consistent-hashing article's load-balancing example hashes an item and takes the value modulo the number of servers n to choose the server.
Using consistent hashing for load balancing in practice needs a number of extensions to its basic technique.

definition.text: Randomized static load balancing simply assigns each task to a randomly chosen server.

facts.text: Wikipedia says this simple method works quite well.
When the number of tasks is known in advance, calculating a random permutation beforehand is more efficient: it avoids communication per assignment and needs no distribution master.
Even with an unknown number of tasks, a pseudo-random assignment generator known to every processor avoids communication.
Its performance, measured as total execution time for a fixed set of tasks, decreases as the maximum task size grows.

definition.text: A load-balancing algorithm is static when it distributes tasks without taking the current state of the system into account.

facts.text: System state means measures such as how loaded, or overloaded, each processor is; a static method instead makes assumptions beforehand, such as arrival times and resource needs of incoming tasks.
The number of processors, their power and communication speeds are known, so the aim is to match a known set of tasks to the available processors to minimize a performance function.
Static techniques are commonly centralized around a router, or master, which distributes the loads and optimizes the performance function.
They are easy to set up and can be efficient for fairly regular tasks, such as processing HTTP requests from a website.
Statistical variance in how tasks are assigned can still overload some computing units.
Static distribution is always possible even when task execution time is unknown in advance; round robin and random assignment are examples.

definition.text: Dynamic load balancing takes the current load of each computing unit, or node, into account when distributing tasks.

facts.text: Tasks can be moved from an overloaded node to an underloaded node so they are processed faster.
Dynamic algorithms are much more complicated to design but can improve performance, particularly when execution time varies greatly from task to task.
They are usually more general and more efficient than static ones, but they require nodes to exchange information, at the risk of lost efficiency.
The architecture can be more modular, since no specific node has to be dedicated to distributing work.
An algorithm that needs too much communication to reach its decisions risks slowing down the overall solution.
In a unique assignment a task is placed once according to the state at that moment; in dynamic assignment tasks can be redistributed continually as the system evolves.
ByteByteGo's dynamic algorithms are least connections and least response time.

definition.text: In a master-worker scheme a master distributes the workload to workers, and it is among the simplest dynamic load balancing algorithms.

facts.text: Workers start idle and report that to the master; the master answers their requests with tasks and tells them to stop asking when no tasks remain.
The scheme distributes work evenly when the overhead of assigning tasks is low.
It scales poorly: the heavy communication makes it hard to adapt to many processors, and the master acts as a bottleneck.
Replacing the master with a task list shared by the processors improves it, though it is slightly harder to implement and still insufficient for very large computing centers.

title: Work stealing
article: Load balancing (computing)#Non-hierarchical architecture, without knowledge of the system: work stealing

definition.text: Work stealing gives each processor some tasks in a random or predefined way, then lets idle processors steal work from active or overloaded ones.

facts.text: It is a technique for overcoming scalability problems when the time needed to complete tasks is unknown.
Idle processors send requests to random other processors; one that can subdivide its task sends part of its work to the requester, otherwise it returns an empty task.
It can be very effective but is hard to implement, because communication must not become the processors' main occupation.
When the network is heavily loaded it is more efficient for the least loaded units to offer help; when lightly loaded, overloaded processors ask for support. This rule of thumb limits messages.

definition.text: In client-side random load balancing, the client receives a list of server IP addresses and randomly selects one from it on each connection.

facts.text: It relies on all clients generating similar loads, and on the law of large numbers, to give a reasonably flat distribution of load across servers.
The list can be delivered as a DNS list, without any round-robin, or hardcoded in the client.
It has been claimed to distribute load better than round-robin DNS, because large DNS caches skew round-robin results while random client selection is unaffected.
A smart client that detects a failed server and picks again at random also provides fault tolerance.

definition.text: DNS load balancing configures a domain in the Domain Name System so that client requests to the domain are spread across a group of server machines.

facts.text: In round-robin DNS, several IP addresses are tied to one domain name and clients are given them in rotation, with no dedicated software or hardware node needed.
The addresses are given a short expiration, so a client is more likely to use a different IP next time it accesses the service.
A single hostname can resolve to many IP addresses, and servers may rotate the order of the returned set, to spread load and tolerate faults.
Its main weakness is that DNS does not check for server or network outages, so it keeps returning the same IP addresses even when servers are down.

definition.text: In DNS delegation, the website's name is delegated as a sub-domain whose zone is served by the same servers that serve the website.

facts.text: The zone file for the name differs on each server, so each server answers with its own IP address as the A record.
When a server is down its DNS does not respond, so the web service sends it no traffic; if its line is congested, DNS unreliability means less HTTP traffic reaches it.
The quickest DNS response nearly always comes from the closest server, giving geo-sensitive balancing; it works particularly well when servers are spread geographically.
A short TTL on the A record helps divert traffic quickly when a server goes down, but clients may switch between servers in the middle of a session.

definition.text: Sticky sessions, also called persistence or stickiness, send all requests from one user session consistently to the same backend server.

facts.text: The problem: session information stored locally on one backend server cannot be found by requests that land on other backend servers.
If the lost data is only cached information that can be recomputed, using a different server just costs performance.
ByteByteGo lists session persistence and user stickiness as uses of a load balancer, for applications that need a user's session kept on a specific server.
Sticky round-robin improves round robin this way: once a user's first request goes to one service, that user's later requests go there too.
The main downside is no automatic failover: if the backend server goes down, its per-session information becomes inaccessible and the sessions depending on it are lost.
Assignment may be based on username, client IP address or random choice; IP-based assignment can be unreliable because DHCP, network address translation and web proxies change the perceived address.
Random assignments must be remembered by the balancer, a storage burden that can be lost if it fails, and they need client-side state, which fails when cookies are disabled.
Sophisticated load balancers combine several persistence techniques to avoid the shortcomings of any one method.

definition.text: Externalized session state keeps session data outside the individual backend servers, so any server behind the load balancer can handle any request.

facts.text: Ideally the servers behind the balancer are not session-aware, so a client reaching any backend has the same experience; this is usually achieved with a shared database or an in-memory session store such as Memcached.
Session data in a database adds load to it, since databases suit less transient data; the database is often replicated, with load balancing spreading queries over the replicas.
For a browser client, the data can live in the browser, in a time-stamped, encrypted cookie or by URL rewriting; this is generally preferred because the balancer can then pick any backend server.
Client-side storage can be unsuitable when the session state is large and recomputing it on every request is not feasible, and URL rewriting has major security issues because users can alter the URL.

definition.text: A health check is how a load balancer determines whether a server is down or performing poorly, so it can remove that server from the pool.

facts.text: The balancer polls servers for application-layer health and removes failed servers from the pool.
Components are monitored continually, for example web servers by fetching known pages; when one becomes unresponsive the balancer stops sending it traffic.
When a component comes back online, the load balancer starts routing traffic to it again.
ByteByteGo describes continuous evaluation of instances, with requests directed only to fully operational ones and failed or unhealthy servers removed from the pool.

definition.text: Failover is the continuation of service after the failure of one or more of its components, and load balancing is often used to implement it.

facts.text: A load balancer can reroute traffic away from failed or unhealthy servers to healthy ones, so service continues without interruption.
This works only if at least one component exceeds the service's capacity (N+1 redundancy).
N+1 redundancy can be much less expensive and more flexible than pairing every live component with a single backup that takes over (dual modular redundancy).
When available servers drop below a set number or load gets too high, standby servers can be brought online.
With two Internet links, failover uses the second only if the primary fails, while load balancing keeps both in use all the time, which also increases available bandwidth.
The technique can make the load balancer itself a single point of failure.

definition.text: Because a load balancer can itself be a single point of failure, a second or N load balancers can be run together in a cluster.

facts.text: With failure detection, a passive balancer can take over when the active one fails, making the system more fault-tolerant.
Wikipedia notes that balancers are usually implemented as high-availability pairs, which may also replicate session persistence data if the application needs it.
Some balancers can forward to a backup load balancer when all backend servers are unavailable.

definition.text: TLS termination lets the load balancer handle the encryption and decryption of secure connections so the backend servers do not have to.

facts.text: The balancer terminates TLS connections and passes HTTPS requests to the web servers as plain HTTP; if it is not overloaded, users do not notice a slowdown.
Without offloading, encryption and authentication can become a major part of a web server's CPU demand, and users see slower responses as demand grows.
The downside is that all TLS processing concentrates on one device that can become a new bottleneck; adding a few web servers may be cheaper than expensive dedicated hardware.
Terminating TLS at the balancer also lets it balance or switch content based on data in the HTTPS request.

definition.text: Load balancers generally operate at one of two levels: the transport layer, layer 4, or the application layer, layer 7.

facts.text: A layer 4 balancer routes on networking information such as IP addresses and cannot do content-based routing; ByteByteGo adds that it also decides by TCP and UDP ports.
Layer 4 balancers are often dedicated hardware devices that operate at high speed.
A layer 7 balancer can read requests in their entirety and perform content-based routing, managing load with a full understanding of the traffic.
Most balancers can route by the requested URL, provided the request is unencrypted or HTTPS is terminated (decrypted) at the balancer.

definition.text: Content-based routing inspects the message content of a request, so requests can be distributed by something such as the value of a parameter.

facts.text: Singh lists host-based, path-based and content-based routing as common variations of workload distribution.
Host-based routing distributes requests by requested hostname; path-based routing uses the entire URL instead of just the hostname.
Most balancers can send requests to different servers based on the URL requested, if the request is unencrypted or the HTTPS request is terminated at the balancer.
ByteByteGo's platform-specific routing sends requests from different device types, such as mobiles and desktops, to specialized backend systems.

definition.text: Load balancers come in several types, including hardware, software, cloud-based and DNS-based.

facts.text: A hardware load balancer relies on physical, on-premises hardware; it handles a large volume of traffic but often has a hefty price tag and is fairly limited in flexibility.
Hardware balancers include proprietary firmware that needs maintenance and updates as new versions and security patches are released.
Software balancers are usually easier to deploy, more cost-effective and more flexible than hardware, though that flexibility may mean more setup work.
Unlike the closed-box hardware approach, software balancers allow more freedom to change and upgrade, and come as installable solutions or a managed cloud service.
Cloud-based balancers are provided by cloud providers and integrated into their infrastructure, such as AWS Elastic Load Balancer, Google Cloud Load Balancing and Azure Load Balancer.
DNS load balancing spreads client requests for a domain across a group of servers, but it does not check for server or network outages.

definition.text: Global server load balancing distributes traffic across multiple geographic locations to improve redundancy and performance on a global scale.

facts.text: In content delivery, traffic is shared among servers or web caches by service-based (global) or hardware-based (layer 4 to 7 switch) load balancing.
ByteByteGo's cross-zone load balancing spreads incoming traffic across geographic or network zones, raising resilience and capacity for large request volumes.
DNS delegation can give geo-sensitive balancing, because the quickest DNS response nearly always comes from the network's closest server.

definition.text: Beyond spreading requests by a scheduling algorithm, hardware and software load balancers may offer a variety of special features, most of them vendor specific.

facts.text: Singh lists autoscaling, sticky sessions, health checks, persistent connections such as WebSocket, TLS handling, certificates, compression, caching, logging, request tracing, redirects and fixed responses.
HTTP compression reduces transferred data and helps more for larger responses and more distant clients, but adds CPU demand on the balancer.
A balancer can cache static content to answer some requests without contacting servers, and buffer responses to slow clients so web servers free their threads sooner.
Against SYN flood attacks, balancers can use SYN cookies and delayed binding, so back-end servers do not see a client until its TCP handshake finishes.

definition.text: In data center networks, load balancing distributes traffic across the many existing paths between any two servers.

facts.text: It allows more efficient use of network bandwidth and reduces provisioning costs.
Static balancing hashes a flow's source and destination addresses and port numbers to choose a path; dynamic balancing assigns flows to paths by monitoring bandwidth use on them.
Dynamic assignment can be proactive, with the assignment fixed once made, or reactive, with the network logic shifting flows between paths as utilization changes.
